title: War Is Over If You Want It
author: Running the Room
summary: Writing as Running the Room, the author uses England's strong PISA 2025 results to revisit a familiar pattern of motivated reasoning among critics of evidence-informed reform, tracing how goalposts shifted repeatedly as Michaela Community School's results kept improving - from claiming it couldn't open, to claiming its results were a fluke, to dismissing exams themselves as meaningless. The central argument is that PISA 2025's finding of England near the top of international rankings in all three tested domains is a strong, if imperfect, endorsement of a decade-long shift toward direct instruction, knowledge-rich curriculum, and firm behaviour management. The author preempts the likely rebuttal that PISA doesn't matter by pointing out this same test was celebrated uncritically when it favored Finland's progressive model in 2000, arguing critics only distrust the metric when it stops confirming their priors. A closing analogy to medicine - paracetamol and handwashing work regardless of who invented them - is used to argue that evidence for effective teaching methods should be assessed on its merits rather than dismissed for its perceived political origin.
points: Documents a specific, escalating sequence of goalpost-shifting arguments used against Michaela Community School, from 'it can't open' through 'it's just an exam factory,' as a case study in motivated reasoning against evidence that contradicts prior commitments.

Argues that PISA's credibility with critics has always tracked whether its results flattered their preferred pedagogy, citing the uncritical celebration of Finland's PISA success around 2000 as the mirror image of today's dismissal of England's results.

Frames England's stable PISA 2025 performance against the OECD's broader decline as evidence that a specific policy bundle - direct instruction, knowledge-rich sequencing, behaviour management, and terminal exams - can move system-level outcomes, not just individual school outcomes.

Uses a medicine analogy (paracetamol and handwashing) to separate the political origin of a policy from its empirical effectiveness, arguing evidence should be evaluated independent of who proposed it.
Explicitly concedes PISA's imperfection while still treating it as a meaningful signal worth learning from, resisting both uncritical PISA-worship and reflexive PISA-dismissal.
quotes: Memorably, critics of Michaela Community School used to say it couldn't be opened; then that no one would want to go; then that the method wouldn't work; then that their initial success was a one off; then that replication of the success was a fluke

Their goalposts simply shifted after every goal, and they shift still. By doing so we uncover the motivated reasoning that underpinned the critics: they never believed that schools should try to help children to learn about a broad liberal curriculum, and have that assessed in a meaningful way.

This appears, on the surface, to be a monumental endorsement of the direction of travel over the past decade, with its slow, continuous emphasis on direct instruction, knowledge-rich, carefully sequenced curriculums, behaviour management, and externally-assessed terminal exams.

PISA very much mattered when people were feting Finland in 2000, as that country rode the lightning of success, despite the fact that its success was not in fact down to the progressive woo going on at the time, but the decades of good practices that had been used before that
England has done something mechanically magical: demonstrated how education systems can improve. Not perfectly, not evenly, but nonetheless demonstrated.
Paracetamol and handwashing perform the same role whoever invented them. Biochemistry is neutral. How we learn is too.
We should celebrate this outcome because it represents the success of millions of children throughout England, and their futures, and our national community.
